source_text: Disciplina custos spei, retinaculum fidei, dux itineris salutaris, fomes ac nutrimentum bonae indolis, magistra virtutis, facit in Christo manere semper ac jugiter Deo vivere et ad promissa coelestia et ad divina praemia pervenire. Hanc et sectari salubre est, et aversari ac negligere lethale. In Psalmis loquitur Spiritus sanctus: Continete disciplinam, ne forte irascatur Dominus, et pereatis a via recta, cum exarserit cito ira ejus super vos. Et iterum: Peccatori autem dixit Deus. Ad quid exponis justificationes meas, et assumis testamentum meum per os tuum? Tu autem odisti disciplinam et abjecisti sermones meos retro. Et denuo legimus: Disciplinam qui abjicit, infelix est. Et de Salomone mandata Sapientiae monentis accepimus: Fili, ne neglexeris disciplinam Domini, nec defeceris ab eo correptus; quem enim diligit Deus corripit. Si autem Deus quem diligit corripit et ad hoc corripit ut emendet, fratres quoque, et maxime sacerdotes, non oderunt sed diligunt eos quos corripiunt ut emendent. quando et Deus per Hieremiam ante praedixerit et tempora nostra significaverit dicens: Et dabo vobis pastores secundum cor meum, et pascent vos pascentes cum disciplina. Quod si in Scripturis sanctis frequenter et ubique disciplina praecipitur, et fundamentum omne religionis ac fidei de observatione ac timore profiscitur, quid cupidius appetere, quid magis velle ac tenere nos convenit, quam ut, radicibus fortius fixis, et domiciliis nostris super petram robusta mole solidatis, inconcussi ad procellas et turbines saeculi stemus, ut ad Dei munera per divina praecepta veniamus, considerantes pariter ac scientes quod templa Dei sint membra nostra, ab omni faece contagionis antiquae lavacri vitalis sanctificatione purgata, nec violari ea aut pollui fas sit, quando qui violat et ipse violetur. Eorum nos templorum cultores et antistites sumus. Serviamus illi cujus esse jam coepimus. Paulus in Epistolis suis dicit quibus nos ad curricula vivendi per divina magisteria formavit: Non estis vestri. Empti enim estis pretio magno. Clarificate et portate Deum in corpore vestro Clarificemus et portemus Deum puro et mundo corpore et observatione meliore; et qui per sanguinem Christi redempti sumus, per omnia servitutis obsequia Redemptoris imperio pareamus, demusque operam ne quid immundum et profanum templo Dei inferatur, ne offensus sedem quam inhabitat derelinquat. Sospitantis Domini verba sunt et docentis, curantis pariter et monentis: Ecce, inquit, sanus factus es, jam noli peccare, ne quid tibi deterius fiat. Dat vivendi tenorem, dat innocentiae legem, postquam contulit sanitatem; nec habenis liberis et solutis vagari postmodum patitur, sed ipsis potius quibus sanatus fuerat mancipato gravius comminatur, quod sit scilicet minor culpa deliquisse ante cum necdum nosses disciplinam Dei, nulla sit venia ultra delinquere postquam Deum nosse coepisti. Et quidem hoc tam viri quam mulieres, tam pueri quam puellae, sexus omnis atque omnis aetas observet, et curet, pro religione et fide quam Deo debet, ne quod sanctum et purum de Domini dignatione percipitur, minus sollicito timore teneatur. Nunc nobis ad virgines sermo est; quarum quo sublimior gloria est, major et cura est. Flos est ille ecclesiastici germinis, decus atque ornamentum gratiae spiritalis, laeta indoles, laudis et honoris opus integrum atque incorruptum, Dei imago respondens ad sanctimoniam Domini, illustrior portio gregis Christi. Gaudet per illas atque in illis largiter floret Ecclesiae matris gloriosa foecunditas; quantoque plus copiosa virginitas numero suo addit, tanto plus gaudium matris augescit. Ad has loquimur, has adhortamur affectione potius quam potestate; non quod, extremi et minimi et humilitatis nostrae admodum conscii, aliquid ad censuram licentiae vindicemus, sed quod, ad sollicitudinem magis cauti, ptus de diaboli infestatione timeamus. Neque enim inanis haec cautio est et vana formido quae ad salutis viam consulit, quae Dominica et vitalia praecepta custodit, ut quae se Christo dicaverint, et a carnali concupiscentia recedentes tam carne quam mente se Deo voverint, consumment opus suum magno praemio destinatum, nec ornari jam aut placere cuiquam nisi domino suo studeant, a quo et mercedem virginitatis expectant, dicente ipso: Non omnes capiunt verbum, sed illi quibus datum est. Sunt enim spadones qui ex utero matris sic nati sunt, et sunt spadones qui coacti sunt ab hominibus, et sunt spadones qui se ipsos castraverunt propter regnum coelorum. Denuo quoque per hanc Angeli vocem continentiae munus ostenditur, virginitas praedicatur: Hi sunt qui cum mulieribus se non coinquinaverunt. Virgines enim permanserunt. Hi sunt qui sequuntur Agnum quocumque ierit. Neque enim tantum masculis continentiae gratiam Dominus repromittit et feminas praeterit, sed, quoniam femina viri portio est et ex eo sumpta atque formata est, in Scripturis fere omnibus ad protoplastum Deus loquitur, quia sunt duo in carne una et in masculo simul significatur et femina.
pass_a_gloss: Discipline is the guardian of hope, the restraint of faith, the leader of the path of salvation, the nourishment of good character, the teacher of virtue, and it makes us always remain in Christ and live for God, and it brings us to the heavenly promises and divine rewards. It is healthy to follow this discipline, and it is deadly to turn away from and neglect it. The Holy Spirit speaks in the Psalms, saying, 'Keep discipline, lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the right way, when his anger burns quickly over you.' And again, 'To the sinner, God said, Why do you explain my justifications and take my covenant upon your mouth? You, however, hate discipline and reject my words behind your back.' We also read, 'He who rejects discipline is unhappy.' And from Solomon's Wisdom, we receive the command, 'My son, do not neglect the discipline of the Lord, nor fail when he corrects you, for he whom God loves, he corrects.' If God, who loves, corrects and does so in order to improve, then brothers, and especially priests, do not hate but love those they correct so that they may improve. For God, through Jeremiah, previously foretold and indicated our times, saying, 'I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they will feed you, feeding with discipline.' Since discipline is frequently and everywhere commanded in the holy Scriptures, and the foundation of all religion and faith proceeds from its observation and fear, what should we more eagerly desire, what should we more wish to hold, than that, with our roots more firmly fixed and our houses built upon a strong rock, we may stand unshaken against the storms and whirlwinds of the world, so that we may come to God's gifts through divine precepts, considering and knowing that our bodies are temples of God, purified from all the filth of ancient contamination by the sanctification of the living water, and that it is not right for them to be violated or polluted. We are the cultivators and priests of these temples. Let us serve the one whose we have begun to be. Paul, in his Epistles, says to those whom he formed for the courses of living through divine teachings, 'You are not your own, for you have been bought with a great price. Clarify and carry God in your body.' Let us clarify and carry God in a pure and clean body and with better observance, and we, who have been redeemed through the blood of Christ, let us obey the command of the Redeemer through all the services of servitude, and let us take care that nothing unclean and profane be brought into the temple of God, lest the Lord, who is offended, abandon the seat he inhabits. The words of the Lord, who saves, teaches, cares, and warns, are, 'Behold, you have been made healthy, do not sin anymore, lest something worse happen to you.' He gives the tenor of living, the law of innocence, after he has given health, and he does not allow us to wander afterward with free and loose reins, but rather, he threatens more severely those whom he has healed, because it is a lesser fault to have sinned before when one did not yet know the discipline of God, and there is no forgiveness for sinning after one has begun to know God. And indeed, this should be observed and cared for by both men and women, by both boys and girls, of all sex and age, for the sake of the religion and faith that we owe to God, lest what is holy and pure, received from the Lord's dignity, be held with less solicitous fear. Now our speech is to virgins, whose glory is more sublime, and whose care is greater. They are the flower of the ecclesiastical germ, the ornament of spiritual grace, a joyful character, a work of praise and honor, whole and uncorrupted, the image of God responding to the Lord's sanctity, a more illustrious part of Christ's flock. The glorious fertility of the Church, our mother, rejoices and flourishes abundantly through them, and the more numerous the virgins are, the more the mother's joy increases. We speak to them, we exhort them with affection rather than power, not because, being extremely humble and conscious of our humility, we claim anything for the censure of license, but because, being more cautious, we fear the devil's temptation. For this caution is not empty and vain, which consults for the path of salvation, which keeps the Lord's and vital precepts, so that those who have dedicated themselves to Christ and, receding from carnal desire, have vowed themselves to God in both flesh and mind, may consummate their work, destined for a great reward, and may not strive to be adorned or pleasing to anyone except their Lord, from whom they also expect the reward of virginity, he himself saying, 'Not all receive the word, but those to whom it is given.' For there are eunuchs who were born so from their mother's womb, and there are eunuchs who were made so by men, and there are eunuchs who have castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Again, through the voice of the Angels, the gift of continence is shown, and virginity is preached: 'These are those who have not defiled themselves with women, for they have remained virgins. These are those who follow the Lamb wherever he goes.' For the Lord does not promise the grace of continence only to men and pass over women, but since woman is a part of man and was taken and formed from him, in almost all the Scriptures, God speaks to the first-formed man, because the two are one flesh, and both the male and the female are signified in the male.

bible_refs.note: Eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven

pass_b_english: Discipline guards hope, restrains faith, leads the way of salvation, feeds and nurtures a good character, and teaches virtue; it keeps us always in Christ, makes us live for God, and brings us to the heavenly promises and divine rewards. To follow it is healthy; to turn away and neglect it is deadly. The Holy Spirit speaks in the Psalms: 'Keep discipline, lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the right way, when his anger burns quickly over you' (Psalm 2:12). And again: 'To the sinner God said, Why do you recite my justifications and take my covenant on your lips? You hate discipline and cast my words behind you.' We also read: 'Whoever rejects discipline is unhappy.' From Solomon's Wisdom we receive the command: 'My son, do not neglect the Lord's discipline, nor lose heart when he corrects you; for the Lord disciplines the one he loves' (Proverbs 3:11-12). Since God corrects those he loves in order to improve them, brothers, and especially priests, do not hate but love those they correct, so that they may improve. Through Jeremiah God foretold our times, saying: 'I will give you shepherds after my own heart, and they will feed you with discipline' (Jeremiah 3:15). Because discipline is commanded everywhere in holy Scripture, and the whole foundation of religion and faith springs from observing and fearing it, what should we desire more eagerly, what should we wish for and hold more firmly, than that, with our roots fixed more deeply and our houses built solidly on rock, we may stand unshaken against the world's storms and whirlwinds, and so come to God's gifts through his divine precepts? We consider and know that our bodies are temples of God, washed clean from every stain of ancient defilement by the sanctification of living water, and that they must not be violated or polluted; the one who violates them will himself be violated (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). We are the stewards and priests of these temples. Let us serve the One to whom we now belong. Paul writes in his Epistles to those he has shaped for the race of life through divine teaching: 'You are not your own; you were bought at a great price. Glorify God in your body' (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). Let us glorify and carry God in a pure and clean body with better observance. We who have been redeemed by Christ's blood must obey our Redeemer's command through every service of slavery, and take care that nothing unclean or profane enters God's temple, lest the offended Lord abandon the seat he inhabits. The Savior's words are those of a teacher, healer, and warning voice: 'See, you are well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you' (John 5:14). He gives a rule of life and a law of innocence after granting health; he does not let us wander afterward with loose reins, but threatens more severely those he has healed, because it is a lesser fault to have sinned before knowing God's discipline, but there is no excuse for sinning after one has begun to know God. This must be observed and guarded by men and women, boys and girls, every sex and every age, for the sake of the religion and faith we owe God, so that what is holy and pure, received from the Lord's goodness, is not held with less careful reverence. Now my address turns to virgins, whose glory is more sublime and whose care is greater. They are the flower of the Church's seed, the ornament of spiritual grace, a joyful nature, a complete and uncorrupted work of praise and honor, God's image answering to the Lord's sanctity, a more illustrious portion of Christ's flock. The glorious fruitfulness of our mother the Church rejoices and flourishes abundantly through them; the more virgins increase in number, the more the mother's joy grows. I speak to them, I exhort them with affection rather than authority, not because I, the least and lowliest, keenly aware of my humility, claim any right to censure, but because, being more cautious, I fear the devil's assaults. This caution is not empty or vain; it looks to the way of salvation, it keeps the Lord's vital precepts, so that those who have dedicated themselves to Christ, turning from carnal desire, have vowed themselves to God in both flesh and mind, may complete their work destined for a great reward, and strive to adorn and please no one but their Lord, from whom they await the reward of virginity, he himself saying: 'Not all can accept this word, but only those to whom it is given. For there are eunuchs who were born that way, and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by men, and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven' (Matthew 19:11-12). Again, through the angels' voice the gift of continence is shown and virginity proclaimed: 'These are those who have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins. These follow the Lamb wherever he goes' (Revelation 14:4). The Lord does not promise the grace of continence only to men and pass over women; since woman is a part of man, taken and formed from him, in almost all Scripture God speaks to the first-formed man, because the two are one flesh, and both male and female are signified in the male (Genesis 2:21-24).

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text, including the complex theological arguments regarding discipline, the body as a temple, and the specific exhortations to virgins. All scripture citations in Pass B correspond correctly to the Latin text and the implied biblical passages (e.g., Jeremiah 3:15, Matthew 19:11-12, Revelation 14:4, Genesis 2:21-24).
